story: In December 1971, the Soviet Mars 3 probe achieved history by making the first successful soft landing on the Red Planet. But triumph instantly turned to mystery. Just seconds after touching down, the lander began transmitting its first views of the Martian surface, only to abruptly cut out forever after transmitting for roughly fourteen to twenty seconds. The only data ever recovered was a partial, featureless gray image. For decades, the fate of the lander remained entirely unknown, trapped beneath a raging, planet-wide dust storm that may have triggered a fatal electrical discharge. But the story didn't end there. In 2013, Russian space enthusiasts using crowdsourced data scoured high-resolution images taken by NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and actually spotted the long-lost lander hardware, its parachute, and heat shield sitting right on the Martian surface, finally solving a decades-old space mystery.
angle: The first spacecraft to successfully land on Mars transmitted for less than twenty seconds before going silent forever—and was only rediscovered decades later by amateur sleuths combing through NASA photos online.

claims.claim: Mars 3 was launched by the Soviet Union on May 28, 1971.
The Mars 3 descent module achieved a soft landing on Mars on December 2, 1971.
Mars 3 became the first spacecraft to successfully make a soft landing on Mars.
The Mars 3 lander transmitted data from the surface for only 14.5 to 20 seconds before cutting out.
The only image returned by the lander was a partial, featureless gray image with no details.
At the time of landing, Mars was enveloped by a massive, planet-wide dust storm.
The exact cause of the lander's sudden transmission failure remains unknown.
In 2013, Russian space enthusiasts and citizen scientists using crowdsourcing located potential hardware of Mars 3 in NASA images.
The images used to find the hardware were captured by the High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) camera on NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.
The identified hardware candidates on the Martian surface include the lander's parachute, heat shield, retrorocket, and the lander itself.
The combined launch mass of the Mars 3 spacecraft including fuel was 4,650 kg.

disputed: Whether the partial image transmitted by the lander shows the Martian horizon or is merely optical noise/gray background should be attributed as a matter of speculation or according to various accounts.

The precise reason for the transmission failure—such as a coronal discharge caused by the dust storm versus a battery or transmitter failure—should be presented as hypotheses or attributed as potential causes.
